economy.short: What moving costs: the oxygen or energy used to go at a given speed or power once oxygen uptake is steady. Lower cost = better economy. It counts only the input, not the work done.

energy-cost.short: The energy used to cover a distance, e.g. kJ per kg per km, worked out from oxygen uptake and RER so that it allows for the fuel being burned.

tendon-stiffness.short: How much force it takes to stretch a tendon. A stiffer tendon stretches less for the same force and, like a firm spring, can store energy and give it back.

leg-stiffness.short: How much the whole leg gives on landing: the peak force on the ground divided by how far the leg compresses. A stiff leg acts like a firm spring, a soft one like a squashy one.

vertical-oscillation.short: How far the body rises and falls with each running stride.

super-shoes.short: Racing shoes with a thick, light, springy foam midsole and a stiff (often carbon) plate, designed to lower the energy cost of running. Also called advanced footwear technology.

force-effectiveness.short: The share of the force on the pedal that pushes at right angles to the crank and so turns it; the rest pushes along the crank and does no work.

torso-angle.short: The angle of a cyclist's back above the horizontal. 0° is a flat back; a lower angle is more aerodynamic but more cramped.

drag.short: The force that water or air pushes back with against something moving through it. It rises steeply with speed.

friction-drag.short: Drag from water (or air) rubbing along the surface of the skin and suit.

pressure-drag.short: Drag from the low-pressure wake behind a body, set by its shape and the area it presents to the water. Also called form drag.

wave-drag.short: Drag from the energy spent making waves when moving at or near the water surface. It mostly disappears well below the surface.

propelling-efficiency.short: The share of a swimmer's mechanical work that actually pushes the body forward, rather than just setting water moving.

distance-per-stroke.short: How far a swimmer travels with each arm cycle (speed ÷ stroke rate). A longer stroke at the same speed usually means a higher propelling efficiency.

plyometrics.short: Explosive jumping and bounding exercises, such as hops and drop jumps, in which muscles and tendons are quickly stretched and then shorten.

one-rep-max.short: The heaviest load you can lift once with good form in a given exercise. Strength-training loads are given as a % of it.

live-high-train-low.short: Sleeping and living at real or simulated altitude, where each breath holds less oxygen, while training near sea level.

heat-acclimation.short: The body's adaptation to repeated exercise in the heat over days to weeks: more plasma volume, earlier and more sweating, lower heart rate and core temperature.

allometric-scaling.short: Dividing a measure by body mass raised to a power (mass^b, e.g. W·kg⁻⁰·³²) instead of by mass itself, because the measure doesn't grow one-to-one with mass.
